echoes.note: Entrusting the deposit to 'faithful men' who can teach others recalls the OT ideal of the trustworthy servant, paradigmatically Moses who is 'faithful in all my house.' The transmission-by-faithful-stewards motif underlies Paul's chain of witnesses.

The soldier who must not be 'entangled in the affairs of life' so he can please his commander echoes the holy-war muster law, which exempts the man who has built a house, planted a vineyard, or betrothed a wife so that the army on campaign is undistracted. The single-minded enlisted soldier is the shared image.

The 'farmers who labor must be first to get a share of the crops' draws on the Torah principle that the one who plants the vineyard rightly enjoys its fruit. The labor-then-reward logic runs through the soldier/athlete/farmer triad.

'He who tends a fig tree will eat its fruit' is the closest sapiential parallel to the laboring farmer who earns the first share. Paul applies the proverb's reward-for-tending logic to gospel ministry.

The right of the agricultural laborer to a share of the produce echoes the ox-treading-grain principle Paul elsewhere applies to ministry support. Faint but thematically continuous with the farmer image.

'Jesus Christ... of the seed of David' invokes the Davidic covenant promise that God will raise up David's offspring and establish his kingdom forever. Paul reads the resurrection as the fulfillment of the dynastic promise of an everlasting seed.
The Davidic-seed Christology resonates with the shoot from the stump of Jesse, the messianic branch of David's line. Combined with v.10's root of Jesse, it grounds the title in prophetic messianism.
The 'root of Jesse' standing as a banner to which the nations rally undergirds the risen seed of David proclaimed in Paul's gospel for the chosen ones. Reinforces the Davidic-messiah background.
'The fruit of your body I will set on your throne' restates the sworn promise of a Davidic heir behind 'of the seed of David.' A liturgical witness to the covenant Paul presupposes.

'If we are faithless, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself' echoes the Song of Moses' confession of God as the faithful Rock, without iniquity, just and upright. Divine constancy despite human failure is the shared theology.

'He cannot deny himself' restates Balaam's oracle that God is not a man that he should lie, nor change his mind; what he has said he will do. The immutability of God's own word grounds the faithful saying.

Paul's endurance 'for the chosen ones' sake' picks up Isaiah's promise that God's chosen/elect will inherit and possess. The remnant-election vocabulary colors the eschatological 'salvation with eternal glory.'

'But God's word isn't chained' faintly echoes the promise that the word going out from God's mouth will not return empty but accomplishes its purpose. The irrepressible, effective word is the common motif against Paul's chains.

'The Lord knows those who are his' quotes Moses' answer to Korah's rebellion, when the Lord makes known who is his and who is holy. Paul stamps this as the first half of the seal on God's firm foundation amid the disruption of false teachers (Hymenaeus, Philetus) — a deliberate Korah typology of schism within the covenant community.

'Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from unrighteousness' draws directly on Moses' command to depart from the tents of the wicked men (Korah, Dathan, Abiram) lest one be swept away in their sins. The Korah scene supplies both halves of the v.19 double seal: God knows his own, and the faithful must separate from the rebels.

'Everyone who names the name of the Lord' echoes Isaiah's confession that only your name we acknowledge/invoke, contrasting the true God with other lords who ruled. Supplies the naming-the-Name half of the citation alongside the Korah command.

'Depart from unrighteousness' resonates with the exodus-from-Babylon summons, 'Depart, depart, touch no unclean thing... be clean, you who bear the vessels of the Lord.' The separation-and-purity demand (and the vessel imagery picked up in vv.20-21) makes this a strong secondary source for the seal.
'Depart from unrighteousness/iniquity' parallels Elihu's word that God commands them to return from iniquity. A sapiential analogue to the moral-separation clause.

'Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity' supplies a Psalter idiom of separation from the wicked that the v.19 seal recasts as an imperative on those who name the Name. Faint and one of several possible backgrounds.

The potter who from the same clay molds both vessels for clean uses and their opposites, deciding the use of each, is the closest antecedent to the great house with vessels for honor and dishonor. Strong deuterocanonical parallel for the honorable/dishonorable distinction.

The potter reworking the clay 'as it seemed good to him,' with God's sovereign right over the house of Israel like clay in the potter's hand, underlies the vessels-for-honor-or-dishonor image and the call to be made fit for the master's use.

'Shall the thing made say of its maker, He did not make me?' frames the made vessel's subordination to its fashioner, the conceptual ground for a vessel cleansing itself for honorable use under the master.

'Woe to him who strives with his Maker... shall the clay say to the potter, What are you making?' reinforces the potter-and-clay sovereignty motif behind the honor/dishonor vessels. Pairs with 29:16 as the prophetic clay backdrop.

As clay is in the potter's hand to mold as he pleases, so humanity is in the hand of the Maker who appoints some for honor and some for dishonor — verbal and conceptual proximity to vessels for honor and dishonor in a household.

Belshazzar's praise of gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone supplies the closest OT catalogue of vessel materials (here gold, silver, wood, clay). The list of materials, not the theology, is the link.

The purity rules distinguishing vessels of wood and clay and requiring cleansing or breaking faintly inform 'if anyone purges himself... he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified.' The clean-vessel cultic background colors the sanctification language.

Calling on the Lord 'out of a pure heart' echoes the ascent liturgy's requirement of clean hands and a pure heart to stand in God's holy place. The pure-heart qualification for approaching God is the shared demand.

'Those who call on the Lord' draws on the promise that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved, the OT formula for the worshipping covenant people. Paul restricts it to those who call from a pure heart.
'Pursue righteousness... and peace' echoes the wisdom imperative to depart from evil, do good, and seek peace and pursue it. The verb 'pursue' applied to peace is a notable verbal contact.
'Pursue righteousness' resonates with Isaiah's address to those who pursue righteousness and seek the Lord. A secondary prophetic backdrop to the chain of virtues to pursue.

'The Lord's servant must not quarrel but be gentle... patient' echoes the Servant of the Lord who will not cry out or lift up his voice in the street and will not break a bruised reed. The non-contentious, gentle servant typology shapes the ideal teacher.
'Flee youthful lusts' faintly recalls the verdict that the inclination of the human heart is evil from youth. The youth-as-locus-of-sinful-impulse motif lies behind the warning.
Recovering 'out of the devil's snare' having been 'taken captive' echoes deliverance from the snare of the fowler. The trap-and-rescue imagery supplies the OT coloring for the diabolical snare.

God's giving 'repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth' parallels the affirmation that God judges gradually and gives room/opportunity for repentance. A deuterocanonical analogue to the divine grant of repentance.
